Watts writes for ladies who already hold needle and thread, and her directions assume a working knowledge of the craft. The book preserves the home needlework of its age in exact detail. It still serves makers who like period patterns and plain, step-by-step instruction.
3454-the-lilac-fairy-book:
Andrew Lang edits this volume of fairy tales, one of his famous colored fairy books for children. In his preface he answers the dinner party question he hears most often, whether he is writing another fairy book. He answers with the same patience he gives to lawyers, dentists, and clergymen asked about their work. The tales that follow come from many lands and many storytellers.

Inside are princes and witches, clever youngest children, enchanted animals, and quests that reward kindness and courage. Lang keeps the stories short and plain, so they read well aloud at bedtime. The book suits families who want classic tales in their old form, without modern retelling or moral lectures tacked on.
3672-the-2000-cia-world-factbook:
This volume reproduces the Central Intelligence Agency's World Factbook for the year 2000, as prepared for Project Gutenberg by Martin Pedersen from the agency's online edition. It gives short profiles of every country and territory, from Egypt and El Salvador to Fiji, Finland, France, and French Guiana, with facts on geography, people, government, economy, and communications.

Readers should note that the Gutenberg edition omits the original maps and graphics, and that tables may not align perfectly after conversion. The Factbook itself is a reference snapshot, not a narrative, and later editions replaced it online. The volume suits researchers who want a compact, year 2000 picture of the world as American officials summarized it.
48-the-1992-cia-world-factbook:
The Central Intelligence Agency's 1992 Factbook surveys the world country by country. This edition, dated January 1, 1993, keeps the agency's standard pattern for officials. Each entry covers land, people, government, economy, and defense.

Afghanistan opens the alphabetical run, with area compared to Texas and borders listed in detail. Similar entries follow for every recognized state and territory. The 1992 volume catches new states rising from the Soviet collapse. It remains a useful snapshot of that turning year. Researchers pair this edition with the 1990 and 1991 volumes to trace the Soviet breakup. Its country notes still help readers date the new post-Soviet map.
503-the-blue-fairy-book:
Andrew Lang edits this first of his colored fairy books, gathering tales from France, Germany, and the East. Cinderella, Beauty and the Beast, and Aladdin sit beside Hansel and Gretel, Little Red Riding Hood, and Rumpelstiltskin. The Bronze Ring, East of the Sun and West of the Moon, and the Forty Thieves add rarer fare.

Lang retells each tale in clear, lively prose for children, keeping wonder and a touch of fear. The volume set the pattern for his whole series. It endures as a treasury where old tales meet new readers, and where a glass slipper still fits after more than a century.
540-the-red-fairy-book:
Andrew Lang edits this second colored fairy book, gleaning less familiar tales from Norse, French, and German sources. The Twelve Dancing Princesses, Jack and the Beanstalk, Rapunzel, the Golden Goose, and the Story of Sigurd sit beside Drakestail, Mother Holle, and the Seven Foals. Translators, named in the preface, shaped each tale.

Lang hopes these tales, less worn than old friends, will charm anew. His clear prose keeps wonder without preach. The volume endures as a treasury for children and collectors, where a second gleaning proves the fairy field still rich.
5615-the-pink-fairy-book:
Andrew Lang edited The Pink Fairy Book, gathering nursery tales from around the world. His preface notes that all peoples tell such tales to children. Japanese, Chinese, Native Americans by camp fires, Eskimo in winter huts, and South Africans join modern Greeks and old Egyptians, along with Germans, French, Spanish, Italians, Danes, and Highlanders. Stories resemble one another everywhere, Lang observes.

Children who read the Blue, Red, and Yellow Fairy Books will meet old friends with new faces here, alongside fresh tales. Lang's collection favors wonder, wit, and brevity. Readers get a classic fairy book, perfect for reading aloud, with tales gathered across continents.
571-the-1995-cia-world-factbook:
The Central Intelligence Agency's 1995 World Factbook surveys every country and territory in one reference volume. Entries run from Afghanistan to Zimbabwe, with notes on geography, people, government, economy, transport, communications, and defense forces. A search scheme lets readers jump straight to a country or a single category.

The Factbook's plain, tabular style makes it a quick check for basic facts as they stood in 1995. Borders, capitals, and economies have shifted since, so it serves best as a snapshot of its year. Researchers still value it as a baseline for how the world looked just after the Cold War.
6344-the-2002-cia-world-factbook:
The Central Intelligence Agency's World Factbook for 2002 lists every country and territory from Afghanistan to Zimbabwe, with oceans, islands, and disputed places in between. Each entry gives geography, people, government, economy, communications, transport, military, and transnational issues, in the Factbook's compact, factual style. A sample entry shows electricity by source, consumption, exports, and imports, with farm products, exports, and partners listed in figures.

Read as a whole, the volume is a reference snapshot of the world in 2002, before later borders, wars, and censuses changed its numbers. It is not a narrative but a tool, meant for quick lookup and comparison, from cocoa and gold exports to power grids and trade partners. The hosted file preserves that year's country listing in full, a useful baseline for anyone tracing how nations changed after it.
640-the-yellow-fairy-book:
Andrew Lang edits this Yellow Fairy Book, fourth in his colored series after blue, red, and green. The Cat and the Mouse, the Six Swans, the Emperor's New Clothes, the Golden Crab, and Thumbelina lead the set, with the Steadfast Tin Soldier, the Tinder-box, and the Nightingale. A dedication to Joan, Toddles, and Tiny fronts the book.

Lang answers critics of fairy books by appealing to a jury of children, who, he trusts, will acquit him. His prose keeps the tales bright and plain. The volume endures as a beloved treasury, where old tales meet new readers in yellow covers.
641-the-violet-fairy-book:
Andrew Lang edits this Violet Fairy Book, stressing in his preface that he did not invent these tales. Translated from folk tales in many tongues, they tell of the Tontlawald and the finest liar in the world. Three wonderful beggars, the goat's ears of Emperor Trojan, and the maiden with the wooden helmet add more wonder. Old magic stands where science now stands.

Lang writes that such tales are as old as human invention, told by savage mothers to savage children and later dressed with kings and queens. His clear prose keeps their wonder. The volume charms as a treasury of rarer fairy tales, where beasts talk and heroes learn by wit.
6576-the-bobbsey-twins-at-meadow-brook:
Laura Lee Hope sends Nan, Bert, Freddie, and Flossie Bobbsey home from a fine trip, then off again for a summer at Meadow Brook. A crash of crockery opens the fun, and soon the twins face a runaway boy, a lost dog, a picnic, and a haystack hide-and-seek. The chapter list reads like a summer diary, full of small mishaps and quick rescues.

A sham battle, moving pictures, a circus, and a wild animal scare keep the pace lively, while a tale from a boy named Frank ties the loose ends. Hope keeps the talk bright and the danger mild, so young readers can enjoy the scare without fear. The Bobbsey Twins at Meadow Brook is a cheerful summer book for the youngest readers.
6703-favorite-dishes-a-columbian-autogra:
Carrie Shuman compiles more than three hundred autograph recipes, with twenty-three portraits, from the Board of Lady Managers of the World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago, 1893. The noble women behind the Women's Department gave these recipes so the compiler could help women pay the costs of a visit to the fair. Each dish bears its giver's own hand.

The book thus serves as both a cookbook and a souvenir of a great fair, with famous names beside plain, usable dishes. Shuman congratulates the lady managers warmly in her preface. Favorite Dishes is a delightful, historic cookbook, full of 1890s taste and fair-time pride.
6745-miss-parloa-s-new-cook-book:
Maria Parloa, principal of the Boston School of Cooking, offers a guide to marketing and cooking, with pictures. Her preface recalls the Appledore Cook Book of nine years before, written after she saw so many failures and so much mortification from vague directions. Minute steps, she found in teaching, were what cooks truly needed.

This new book keeps that plain, exact method, with marketing advice added to recipes. Parloa writes as a teacher, not a show cook, and her aim is success at home. Miss Parloa's New Cook Book is a classic, practical American cookbook, still clear and useful today.
6746-the-grey-fairy-book:
Andrew Lang edits The Grey Fairy Book, with tales from Lithuania, Africa, Germany, France, Greece, and many other lands. Translators and adapters include Mrs. Dent, Mrs. Lang, Eleanor Sellar, and Miss Blackley. The Three Sons of Hali comes from a French Cabinet des Fées of the last century, with tales nested inside tales, like carved ivory balls.

Lang notes that folk tales mix a set of incidents in endless new patterns, like glass in a kaleidoscope. The grey volume thus offers fresh wonders for children who know the red, blue, and yellow books. The Grey Fairy Book is a rich, world-wide fairy collection, made for reading aloud.
7223-the-belgian-cookbook:
Mrs Brian Luck edited this Belgian cook-book from recipes sent by Belgian refugees from all parts of the United Kingdom in 1915. She notes that British cooking may benefit from Belgian dishes, and she offers the small manual for the workaday and inexperienced mistress and maid, not for millionaires. The perfect cook, she jokes, is often heard of but never found.

Refugee kitchens thus become a quiet act of welcome, turning exile into shared tables and plain, good food. The recipes favour thrift and home skill over display, and the book's wartime origin gives its homely advice a deeper warmth. Readers get Belgian fare in English kitchens, gathered in a time of need.
7277-the-green-fairy-book:
Andrew Lang's Green Fairy Book, the third of his coloured fairy books, follows the Blue and the Red, made because children kept asking for more. Lang tells his friendly reader that the stories are borrowed from many countries: some French, some German, some Russian, some Italian, some Scottish, some English, and one Chinese. However much nations differ about trifles, he writes, they all agree in liking fairy tales.

Men long ago, Lang suggests, were much like children in their minds, and that likeness keeps old tales alive across borders. The green volume gathers its wonders with the same generous hand as its sisters, for reading aloud at bedtime. It stands as a classic treasury of world wonder tales.
7797-the-lady-of-the-aroostook:
William Dean Howells's The Lady of the Aroostook opens in the best room of a farmhouse in the hills of northern Massachusetts, one August morning. An elderly woman rocks in a haircloth chair, an old man drums stubbed fingers and whistles without sound, both dressed in unaccustomed finery.

His fresh-shaven face, black satin stock, and lead-colored straw hat mark a family preparing for a journey. The lady of the title will sail on the Aroostook, and Howells follows her from farm parlor to shipboard society, with his usual gentle comedy of American manners abroad.
7935-ballad-book:
Katharine Lee Bates of Wellesley College edits Ballad Book. It opens with Wordsworth on plaintive numbers flowing for old, unhappy, far-off things and battles long ago. Her preface argues that teaching literature should first wake love and enthusiasm for poetry, since love guarantees wider study.

Early ballads, belonging to the youth of English literature and race, appeal with special power to youth, Bates says. Most men of letters keep a boy's tenderness for these rough, frank, spirited poems. The collection offers students a starting point in the critical study of English verse.
87-the-1993-cia-world-factbook:
The Central Intelligence Agency's 1993 Factbook arrived as a preliminary edition, rough in form but full in scope. A note warns that a neater final edition would follow around October 31, 1993. Redundancies were trimmed to cut storage and search costs.

Country entries still follow the agency pattern: geography, people, government, economy, communications, and defense forces. Afghanistan opens the alphabetical list as usual. The 1993 volume captures new states and shifting borders after the Soviet fall. It remains a working snapshot of a world remade. Its preliminary status makes it a telling record of how reference data reached readers then.
8890-mary-jane-her-book:
Clara Ingram Judson writes Mary Jane, Her Book, illustrated by Frances White, as a series of short episodes in a little girl's life. Contents include the broken doll, don't cry over spilled sugar, helping the robins, father's secret, Mary Jane plays school, and aunt Effie comes to visit. Kewpie and the washing, junior's shower bath, playmate Dorothy, learning to sew, and making ready for the picnic follow. The picnic up Clearwater, going shopping, the paper doll show, the birthday party, and a letter and a trip.

Illustrations catch Mary Jane with clinched fists and a perky plaid ribbon showing amazement, exclaiming over a paper doll that looks like her. Sitting on a rock by a creek. Judson's stories teach kindness, helpfulness, and good humour through everyday mishaps.
907-flying-machines-construction-and-ope:
W. J. Jackman and Thomas H. Russell wrote this practical book on how to build and navigate the modern flying machine. With illustrations, working plans, and plain text, they show the reader the frame, the engine, and the controls, and how a pilot handles wind, balance, and landing.

Jackman, author of books on motorcycling, and Russell write for the amateur builder, not the theorist, and their tone is direct and encouraging. The book captures the moment when flight passed from dream to workshop, and it still interests model makers and historians of early aviation for its plans and its can-do spirit.
9913-the-trail-book:
Mary Austin's 1918 book for children follows Oliver and Dorcas Jane as they find the trail through their own country, hoping it leads to wonderland. Along the way, storytellers explain how the world was made: a buffalo chief, Arrumpa with the mastodon, the coyote, and the corn woman.

Later tales tell of the salt trail, the Tallegewi, and how the Lenni-Lenape came from Shinaki, each tied to a real path across the land. Austin, with pictures by Milo Winter, joins Native American storytelling to American geography. Young readers get adventure, myth, and a map of trails under their feet.
a-chinese-wonder-book: Norman Hinsdale Pitman retells Chinese wonder tales in this illustrated book. Its stories include the golden beetle, the great bell, the strange tale of Doctor Dog, and how footbinding started. Other tales treat a talking fish, bamboo and the turtle, and a mad goose in a tiger forest. Pitman presents old Chinese lore in clear English stories for young readers.
a-florida-sketch-book: Bradford Torrey sketches Florida in a book of nature writing. Its chapters wander the flat woods, the marsh, the beach at Daytona, and the hills along the Hillsborough. A morning at an old sugar mill, the upper St. John's, and walks about Tallahassee follow. Torrey, approaching Jacksonville by rail through endless pine barrens, writes of birds and landscape with care.
a-kindergarten-story-book: Jane Lincoln Hoxie offers a kindergarten story book for young children. Many stories had been told to thousands of children in kindergartens from Boston to Pittsburgh. Their delight assures their appeal to child thought and sympathy. Hoxie inscribes the book to her father, whose evening story hour she remembers best.
a-pr-mvad-szok:
A prémvadászok, published in 1873, is the Hungarian translation of a tale by Jules Verne. Verne's adventure novels traveled fast across Europe, and Hungarian readers met many of them in versions like this one. The book preserves that Hungarian form, in which generations of readers in Hungary first followed Verne's northern adventure.

The story opens on the evening of the seventeenth of March, 1859, at Fort Reliance in the far north. Captain Craventy gives a small fête at the fort, a simple reception for which he has spared no pains. From that remote outpost gathering, the tale of fur hunters and the frozen country begins, in classic Verne fashion.
ballad-book:
Katharine Lee Bates of Wellesley College edited this school anthology of early ballads. Her preface speaks for teachers of English: the classroom is only the vestibule to education, and love of poetry is the surest guarantee of study beyond it. Ballads suit the start, she argues, belonging to the youth of the literature and of the English race. Wordsworth's lines on old, unhappy, far-off things stand as motto.

Texts follow in the old spellings, with battles and betrayals in every stanza. The Dowie Dens of Yarrow gives a sample. A lone fighter comes to wield his brand on Yarrow's banks. He hurts two men and slays three. Then a stubborn knight creeps in behind and pierces him through. Bates shaped generations of American schoolrooms' first taste of the traditional ballad.
britannica-1911-bangkok:
Bangkok is the capital of Siam, on the river Me Nam about twenty miles from its mouth. Until modern times the city stood largely on floating pontoons or on piles along its countless canals, which served as its streets. By 1911 well-planned roads crossed the canals at many points, lined with brick houses.

The royal palace, walled in a bend of the river, forms the centre. A second wall, nearly a mile out, rings the packed city proper, with royal parks to the north and the business quarter, rice mills, and docks to the south. The 1911 Britannica entry notes electric tramways, tree-lined streets lit by electricity, and Buddhist temples scattered all over with coloured tile roofs and gilded spires.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-domesday-book:
Domesday Book records the great survey of England that William the Conqueror ordered in 1085 and 1086. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry explains the name, first found in the Dialogue of the Exchequer about 1176. The English called the survey Domesday, or Day of Judgment, because no holding escaped its inquiry and its verdict on land was final, without appeal.

Native chroniclers resented the inquisition, with one writing that no ox, cow, or swine was left unrecorded. The returns tell who held each parcel in 1085 and in King Edward's time, with its size, nature, and value. The entry points students to Maitland, Round, and Ballard among modern guides to this foundation stone of English history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-przemysl-samb:
This encyclopedia entry treats a Greek Catholic diocese of Western Galicia, in Austria, under its triple name. In truth it is the Diocese of Przemysl of the Greek Rite. Sambor marks only an old contest between Catholics and Orthodox at the time of the churches' union. Sanok never held a bishopric at all. Przemysl itself, a fortified town on the River San, lies fifty-four miles west of Lemberg.

In 1900 it counted 46,350 people, and it held the Cathedral of the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist with the diocesan seminary of the Ruthenian Greek Catholics. Sambor, a manufacturing town on the Dniester ten miles away, counted some 17,350 people in 1900. Sanok, smaller still, lay on the San about twenty-five miles to the south-west. Sources from Lemberg and Vienna histories to the 1910 diocesan directory round out a compact portrait of a borderland church.
doe-osti-2588955-infrared-thermometer-in: Point-and-shoot heat readers got their DOE handbook, and this manual covers the infrared guns. The pages walk through the how-to. The techs get their reference. The guns were infrared. The how-to was walked. The reference was tech.
doe-osti-2997625-efficiency-project-play: Efficiency projects got their playbook, and this DOE text lays out the project approach. The pages detail the methods. The energy managers get their guide. The projects were efficiency. The approach was project. The managers got guides. The approach was detailed.
doe-osti-3376012-cyber-informed-engineer: CIE got workbook-EoT/HoT'd, and this DOE workbook covers train communications. The pages detail the end findings. The security folks get their data. The engineering was cyber-informed. The data were security. The HoT were EoT. The communications were train.
doe-osti-3630799-power-lane-county-elect: Power Lane County got grid-handbooked, and this DOE handbook covers electric grids. The pages detail the power findings. The grid folks get their data. The handbook was county. The data were grid. The Lane were Power. The electric were grid.
favorite-dishes-a-columbian-autograph-so:
Carrie V. Shuman's Favorite Dishes is a Columbian souvenir cookery book. It holds over three hundred autograph recipes, with twenty-three portraits. The recipes were sent in by the World's Columbian Exposition lady managers. Shuman compiled the Chicago volume to help women raise the funds for a visit to the Exposition.

Lady Managers and Lady Alternates from every state and territory sent their own favourite recipes. Alaska was included too, so the book reads as a national album of domestic cookery as much as a manual. Soups, meats, cakes and preserves sit beside the signatures and faces of the women who chose them. Cooks and historians alike will enjoy it as a window onto what accomplished American hostesses actually served in 1893.
flying-machines-construction-and-operati:
W J Jackman and Thomas H Russell wrote Flying Machines: Construction and Operation in 1912 for the novice who wanted to build and navigate the modern aeroplane. Octave Chanute, president of the Aero Club of Illinois and a pioneer glider experimenter, supplied an introductory chapter. The preface promises practical guidance on theory, construction, and operation.

Early chapters trace the two-surface machine from Chanute and the Wrights, compare helicopters, ornithopters, and monoplanes, and give plans for a gliding machine with costs and materials. Later discussion works out wing-tip control by varying surface area at the extremities. Published when flying was still a workshop hobby, the book captures aviation at its most experimental and hopeful.
govdocs-archive_org-mazdean-critique-of-:
The Shkand-Gumanig Vizar, the Doubt-Dispelling Exposition, is a ninth-century Zoroastrian defense of the faith written by Mardanfarrokh, son of Hurmazddad. He wrote in Persia, in a land already ruled by Islam for two centuries, to answer doubts among his fellow Zoroastrians.

The work reasons through God's goodness, the origin of evil, and the claims of rival faiths, including a direct critique of Islam. It is one of the richest surviving works of Zoroastrian theology. One caution: the text in this copy is corrupted by a character-encoding shift, which garbles the reading in places.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CookBook_Cook_B: A promotional flyer from the Delmarva Poultry Industry, Inc. announces the finals of the National Chicken Cooking Contest. The sheet was made to publicize the contest's final round, in which home cooks competed with chicken dishes. Nothing in the surviving record gives the flyer's date or names the finalists, so it stands mainly as a piece of poultry industry publicity from the contest era.
govdocs-archive_org-phantom-gerhard-haup:
Gerhart Hauptmann won the Nobel Prize in Literature, and his 1922 novel Phantom shows his darker side at full strength. Bayard Quincy Morgan translated it into English. The story follows a minor clerk who becomes obsessed with a strange young woman he barely knows.

Hauptmann mixes crime, longing, and mirage as the clerk's fixation pulls his whole life apart, page by page. The novel reads partly as confession and partly as fever dream. It stands as a German classic of the years after the First World War, when many writers were drawn to minds coming loose from ordinary life.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_foia_The_Bolton_B:
John Bolton, Donald Trump's former national security adviser, wrote a memoir called The Room Where It Happened. In June 2020 the Trump administration went to court to try to stop it. A National Security Archive posting from June 19, 2020 covers that fight and places it in a longer line of cases over officials publishing what the government calls classified secrets.

The posting includes documentation of earlier prepublication review cases, the system under which former officials must clear manuscripts before printing. That history is the Archive's contribution: book fights look new each time, but the review machinery is old and its rules shape what the public learns. Readers get both the breaking story of one famous memoir and the background needed to judge the censorship claim behind it.
leaves-from-a-field-note-book:
J. H. Morgan wrote Leaves from a Field Note-Book from his war service. He had served as a Home Office commissioner with the British Expeditionary Force. Macmillan published the book in London and New York.

A field note-book suggests scenes set down near the events themselves. Morgan records soldiers, places, and moments from the front. His motto comes from Proverbs: his delights were with the sons of men. That warmth suits a book of observed human detail. Readers get a staff officer's eye joined to a humane pen. Morgan's official role let him see the war's machinery closely. His notes balance that wide view with small human scenes.
mary-jane-her-book:
Clara Ingram Judson wrote Mary Jane: Her Book for young children. Short chapters follow one small girl through her days at home. The contents list names each small event in plain words.

Mary Jane breaks a doll, spills sugar, and helps the robins. She plays school, learns to sew, and plans a picnic up Clearwater. A birthday party, a letter, and a trip close the book. Each tale turns a small mishap into a kind lesson. Father's secret and a paper doll show add small home drama. Judson keeps each scene short, plain, and close to a child's scale.
mcguffey-s-eclectic-spelling-book:
Alexander H. McGuffey's Eclectic Spelling Book appears here in revised form. A front note asks if readers can still spell pharmacopoeia. Hard words like that were set for sixth grade pupils.

The preface says the book keeps the strengths of the old speller. Webster's marks for sounds replace the old number code. Lessons teach prefixes and suffixes near the end of the book. Pupils learn by rules of sound and sense, not by rote alone. Lessons on each sound mark come early, in drills 36 to 57. Sound, sense, and accent work as one in the plan.
miss-parloa-s-new-cook-book:
Maria Parloa, principal of the School of Cooking in Boston, wrote this guide to marketing and cooking. Her preface explains her method. After seeing many failures in home kitchens, she resolved to give minute directions for everything. Little is left to the cook's judgment, on purpose.

The chapter on marketing teaches buyers to choose meats, fish, and vegetables intelligently. Hundreds of recipes follow, nearly all prepared especially for this book. Soups, salads, entrées, and desserts receive unusual length. Parloa argues that those dishes make a table healthful, economical, and elegant. Her book brought cooking-school standards into ordinary American homes.
nasa-tm-19660025355-failure-information-:
Issued on March 1, 1966, the Failure Information Notebook came from the Quality and Reliability Assurance Laboratory. That laboratory sits at NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama. Numbered SR-QUAL-66-4, it gathers recorded failure information for major parts of the Saturn I launch vehicle and its ground support equipment.

Inside, components from the electrical, electromechanical, and mechanical systems are cataloged with their running times and cycle counts. Qualification test results sit beside failure categories, failure frequencies, and failure rates. Observed mean time before failure is given for each part, and an index lets engineers compare past performance quickly. The notebook was built as a shared reference for judging reliability and predicting how parts would perform in the future.
phebe-her-profession-a-sequel-to-teddy-h:
Anna Chapin Ray's Phebe, Her Profession, a sequel to Teddy: Her Book, is dated 1902. It opens in Helena, where a young man sunk in a brown study is hailed by a small boy. The cherub, clutching a paper bag of candy and a rusty hoop, asks politely how everybody is at his house.

The boy has been kept from walking alone for almost a month for spending his pennies at Jake's candy shop. Charmed, the stranger falls into talk with him. Ray builds her story of Phebe and her circle from such small encounters, in the bright manner of her girls' books.
podcast-dannyjones-uQPAVic3Jok:
Researcher Carl Hayden Smith joins Danny Jones to tell how he was injected with DMT so teams could study the fabric of reality. Smith works on how tech and drugs shift the sense of self. He speaks as a test subject here.

Smith tells what the drug showed him, step by step, under lab watch. He talks about the beings, the sense of a built world, and what stayed with him after. Jones asks how a lab can use such wild reports as data. Listeners get a rare first hand lab tale. The library holds the talk as an archive record of his account.
podcast-joerogan-zv8pjyJH4Ok:
Dr. Gabor Mate talks trauma and healing with Joe Rogan in episode 1869 of the Joe Rogan Experience. Mate, a Canadian physician, argues that addiction and many illnesses grow out of early wounds. His book The Myth of Normal questions what modern life does to body and mind.

Mate explains his method of compassionate inquiry, asking patients what happened to them rather than what is wrong with them. He shares stories from his work with addicts in Vancouver's hardest streets. Rogan asks about his own habits and stresses under that lens. The talk offers a gentle, searching view of pain and recovery.
podcast-tuckercarlson-HzHSK7WXqok:
A Gold Star father joins Tucker Carlson to accuse the Biden team of shameful conduct. His son died in service, and grief fuels every word. His quote gives the episode its title: we were used.

He describes the return of the fallen and the words of officials. He says leaders staged honor while dodging blame for a failed exit. Carlson lets the father's anger run without softening it. The episode honors the dead through a parent's charge. It will hit hardest with military families who feel their loss was mishandled.
putnam-s-word-book:
Putnam's Word Book, by Louis A. Flemming, is a writer's aid to an exact and varied vocabulary, copyrighted in 1913 by G. P. Putnam's Sons. It first appeared under the title Synonyms, Antonyms, and Associated Words, and its lists group words with their near matches and related terms.

A long list of short forms opens the book. It marks parts of speech. It names fields such as botany, chemistry, medicine, and music. It also gives the source tongues of words, from French and German to Hebrew and Spanish. A note adds that further words, with their synonyms, stand in an addenda that begins on page 615.
sleep-book:
Leolyn Louise Everett gathered Sleep-Book, subtitled Some of the Poetry of Slumber, printed at New York by the Watkins Company in 1910. Only three hundred and twenty copies were made, on hand-made Van Gelder paper. Everett gives the book to Ethel Du Fré Houston, who, she says, brought the joy and beauty of dream into many lives.

The first piece, signed by Everett, speaks straight to a restless heart. It bids the heart be still, tells the soul to drop the cares and stir of the day, and asks night to take the sleeper into her own calm. A second piece then hails sleep as a soft-breathing god whose downy wing flutters near.
the-1990-cia-world-factbook: The World Factbook 1990 was made each year by the Central Intelligence Agency. It was made for the use of United States government staff. Its style and scope were shaped to their needs. This copy is the electronic form. Its contents list runs to 249 entries. Nations, dependent areas, and other entities fill the list. It runs from Afghanistan and Albania onward. Oceans and polar lands stand in the same roll.
the-1991-cia-world-factbook: The CIA World Factbook 1991 is dated October 15, 1991. Search tags open the copy. They mark country names and section heads. Geography, People, Government, and Economy are the heads named. Single facts gain marks of their own. A front note states the book's source. The Central Intelligence Agency makes it each year. It is made for United States government staff. Facts came from the Bureau of the Census and the Defense Intelligence Agency. The Department of State and other named sources helped as well.
the-1992-cia-world-factbook:
The CIA World Factbook 1992 appears here in a Project Gutenberg printing dated January 1, 1993, set in plain ASCII with search marks for each land and topic. A front note explains how to find a country and each of its sections, from Geography to Defense Forces.

Entries then start with Afghanistan, whose geography is given in full. Its total area is 647,500 square kilometers, a bit smaller than Texas, with 5,529 kilometers of land borders and no coastline at all. Disputes noted include the Pashtunistan issue with Pakistan. Readers get a year-by-year snapshot of every land on earth, in fixed fields that make lands easy to compare.
the-1993-cia-world-factbook: The 1993 CIA World Factbook stands here in a first, rough Gutenberg form. A note flags it as a preliminary edition. A final one was due near midnight on October 31, 1993. The front pages explain search marks for lands and topics. Geography, People, Government, and Economy are the topics named. A contents roll then follows. It runs from Afghanistan onward. New names such as Armenia and Azerbaijan stand in the roll.
the-1994-cia-world-factbook: The 1994 CIA World Factbook opens with search help. An at-sign mark finds each land and topic. Geography, People, Government, and Economy are named. Communications and Defense Forces are named as well. The front pages give copy routes for staff. United States government staff should get copies through their own groups. Sale routes are also listed. They run through the Superintendent of Documents. They run through the Library of Congress DOCEX project. They run through the National Technical Information Service as well.
the-1995-cia-world-factbook: The 1995 CIA World Factbook opens with search help. At-sign marks find each land and topic. Transportation now stands in the topic list. Contents run from publication facts first. Notes on terms and short forms come next. An A-to-Z roll of lands then follows. It starts with Afghanistan. It runs through the Bahamas, Bahrain, and Bosnia and Herzegovina.
the-1997-cia-world-factbook: The 1997 CIA World Factbook opens with a contents list. An introduction comes first. A brief history of basic intelligence and the Factbook follows. Notes and definitions come next. A guide to country profiles follows them. It sets out classes, fields, and subfields. The A-to-Z roll of lands then starts. Afghanistan, Albania, and Algeria head the roll.
the-1998-cia-world-factbook: Dr. Gregory B. Newby prepared the CIA World Factbook 1998 for Project Gutenberg. He took it from the CIA's online version of the book. His note warns that maps are not included. Other graphics from the source are left out as well. Tables may not align well after conversion. They are otherwise intact, he says. The CIA does not keep past Factbooks online. This saved copy may thus serve readers for years.
the-2000-cia-world-factbook: Martin M. Pedersen prepared the CIA World Factbook 2000. He took it from the CIA's online version of the book. His note warns that maps are left out. Graphics are left out as well. Tables may not align after conversion. The CIA does not keep past Factbooks online, he notes. A contents list then follows. It rolls from Afghanistan onward in A-to-Z order. Notes and appendixes follow the country listings.
the-2002-cia-world-factbook: The CIA World Factbook 2002 heads its copy as a country listing. Lands then roll past in A-to-Z order. Afghanistan, Albania, and Algeria come first. The roll runs on through Cambodia and beyond. Oceans stand in the same roll. Polar lands stand there too. Small island areas are mixed in with the rest.
the-belgian-cookbook:
Mrs Brian Luck edited a cookery book in 1915 from recipes sent by Belgian refugees across the United Kingdom. A preface says British cooking may gain from Belgian dishes. The book is aimed at working mistresses and maids, not at millionaires, and most recipes are simple and cheap.

Advice opens each course. Savouries should be small, neat, and alluring, like an ankle. Soup must be very hot and have a good foundation, not a pot of warm water with a cow driven past the door. Fish must be truly fresh, the editor insists, not kept from Saturday to Monday on a false hope.
the-blotting-book:
E. F. Benson published a novel in 1908 that opens on a house of perfect order in Sussex Square, Brighton. Mrs Assheton's rooms are never too hot or cold, meals are always on time, and her Scotch cook never serves a poor dish. Parlour-maids meet guests' wants before they are spoken.

Silver shines, carpets are soft, a billiard table is free of dust, and cigarette boxes stay full. Mrs Assheton, widowed and living alone until her son Morris returned from four years at Cambridge three months earlier, keeps every ceremony even when dining alone. Such smooth formality, presented as self-respect, begs for a crack to appear.
the-blue-fairy-book: Andrew Lang edited The Blue Fairy Book, a large set of folk and fairy tales by many hands. The list of tales runs to more than thirty stories. It holds Little Red Riding-Hood, Cinderella, and the Sleeping Beauty in the Wood. It also holds Aladdin, Beauty and the Beast, Puss in Boots, and Hansel and Gretel. Jack the Giant-Killer, the Forty Thieves, and Blue Beard are there too. The first tale named is The Bronze Ring, though none of the tales is printed in full here.
the-blue-jar-story-book:
The Blue Jar Story Book, dated 1906 from McLoughlin Brothers of New York, holds tales by Maria Edgeworth, Charles Lamb, Mary Lamb, and Alicia Catherine Mant. Its list names six tales in all. They are The Blue Jar, The Basket Woman, The Sea Voyage, The Changeling, The Inquisitive Girl, and The Little Blue Bag.

Edgeworth's title tale starts in London, where a girl of about seven named Rosamond walks with her mother past shop fronts. She sees goods whose names and uses she does not know, and she longs to stop and look. She tells her mother she would be glad to have all the fine things in a toy shop, and her mother asks if she wants them all. The scene sets up a child's wish for more than she needs.
the-bobbsey-twins-at-meadow-brook: Laura Lee Hope wrote The Bobbsey Twins at Meadow Brook, one of her tales of the four Bobbsey young folk. The part names trace a summer stay from a crash of dishes and new plans to a runaway boy and the trip out. Snap's Escape, At Meadow Brook, The Picnic, and Lost in the Hay come next. A sham fight, films, the twins on stage, and a circus crowd the mid parts. Late parts bring Freddie lost and found, Frank's tale, a wild beast scare, a swim, and bad cash.
the-crimson-fairy-book:
Andrew Lang edited The Crimson Fairy Book, written by various hands. His preface admits that each fairy book demands a preface from its editor, and that such pieces are unavoidably dull and useless. Honesty, he says, forces him to keep repeating that he is the editor, not the author, of the tales.

Lang compares his role to that of a man of science toward nature: popular tales are too vast to be the work of one modern mind. The editor's business is to hunt for tales told by peasant or savage grandmothers in many lands, from New Caledonia to Zululand, from polar snows to Greece, Spain, Italy, and far Lochaber.
the-firelight-fairy-book:
Henry Beston wrote The Firelight Fairy Book for young readers, with pictures by Maurice E. Day, printed at Boston in 1919. A short word list at the front explains hard terms like halberd and seneschal.

Beston retells old fairy tales in a warm, fireside voice, keeping the odd speech and dress of the source tales. Kings, guards, spells, and quests fill the pages, with the meanings of strange words set out plainly for children. The book treats fairy lore as a living store of wonder, to be read aloud while the fire burns low and the room grows dark.
the-golden-goose-book:
L. Leslie Brooke made The Golden Goose Book. Frederick Warne and Company printed it in London. It was first printed in 1905. It has many drawings in colour and black and white. The book holds four tales. They are The Golden Goose, The Three Bears, The Three Little Pigs, and Tom Thumb.

The first tale begins in the classic way. A man had three sons. The youngest was called the Simpleton. He was laughed at, scorned, and neglected on all occasions. One day the eldest son wanted to go into the wood. The tale moves off from there. Brooke's retellings keep the old plots. They add his pictures. Those pictures made the book a nursery favourite for young children.
the-green-fairy-book:
Andrew Lang edited The Green Fairy Book. The tales are by various hands. The book is dedicated to Stella Margaret Alleyne. It comes third in the series of Fairy Books of many colours, after the Blue and the Red, and Lang expects it to close the set. Its stories come from many lands: France, Germany, Russia, and Italy all supply some, Scotland and England others, and China one.

The preface argues that tales of this kind are the oldest in the world. Early men, childlike in mind, told each other such stories long before newspapers or novels existed. Grandmothers handed them down to grandchildren. The first ever set down in writing were Egyptian, from near Joseph's time, some three thousand five hundred years ago. Homer shaped tales of the same kind into the Odyssey.
the-grey-fairy-book:
Andrew Lang edited The Grey Fairy Book. The tales are by various hands. His preface says the tales come from many countries. They come from Lithuania and parts of Africa. They come from Germany, France, Greece, and other regions. One tale, The Three Sons of Hali, comes from the old French Cabinet des Fees. It puts tale within tale, like the Eastern balls of carved ivory.

The contents name twenty tales. They open with Donkey Skin and The Goblin Pony. They name The Story of Dschemil and Dachemila, Fortunatus and His Purse, and The Goat-faced Girl. They name The Magician's Horse, The Little Gray Man, and Udea and Her Seven Brothers. They name The White Wolf, Bobino, and The Dog and the Sparrow. The preface argues that popular fiction shakes a fixed stock of incidents into new combinations, like the glass in a kaleidoscope.
the-illustrated-london-reading-book:
The Illustrated London News published this reading book in 1851. Its office stood at 198 Strand. This copy is the third edition. Additions and corrections mark it. The introduction opens with verses on reading well. Few men read or speak with true feeling, they say. The design of the book follows plainly. It aims to strip lessons of their terrors. It strews flowers on the paths to knowledge.

Young readers were to find masterworks inside. Prose and verse from English letters fill the pages. Pictures run throughout the book. A frontispiece shows Prince Albert in his Cambridge robes. He wears the dress of the university's chancellor. The publishers were famous for their pictured newspaper. They brought the same approach to schooling. Drill alone was not their aim. They wanted to charm and move young readers too.
the-kiltartan-history-book: Lady Gregory wrote this history of Ireland in her Kiltartan manner, illustrated by Robert Gregory and aimed at the new university's history classes. Only the title pages and contents are present here. The text itself does not appear. The contents retell the whole sweep in folk style. Ancient times and Goban the builder open them. The Danes and the Battle of Clontarf follow. The English, Henry VIII, and Elizabeth come next. Cromwell's trace and the Battle of Aughrim appear. Patrick Sarsfield, Carolan's song, and Ninety-Eight close the list.
the-lady-of-the-aroostook:
William Dean Howells opens this novel in a farmhouse's best room. Three people sit one August morning in unaccustomed finery. The elderly mother rocks in the haircloth armchair. She calls her husband father. He drums noiseless fingers on the table. His lips pucker to a whistle that makes no sound. His weekly shave leaves frosty stubble in the deeper wrinkles. At the table's other end, their daughter Lyddy leans with face averted. She stares at the hens in the door-yard. She dabs her eyes.

The parents debate the parting in dialect. The mother does not want Lyddy to go. Keeping her home would cost no more than sending her, she says. The father thinks he might recover some passage money. The captain did not seem grasping, he notes. Howells builds his tale from this grief. A country girl voyages to Trieste.
the-lilac-fairy-book:
Andrew Lang edited this fairy tale collection and filled its preface with dinner party complaints. Strangers, he says, always ask a writer what he is writing now. One lady asked if he ever wrote anything but fairy books, and a French expert printed the same claim in a newspaper.

Lang jokes that he should claim a grave treatise on potato blight instead of answering. Behind the teasing stands a serious gatherer of tales from many lands. The lilac volume closes his color fairy book series, drawing stories from Portuguese, Irish, Welsh, and other sources for child and adult readers.
the-little-tea-book:
Arthur Gray compiled The Little Tea Book, published by the Baker and Taylor Company in New York in 1903 with illustrations by George W. Hood. Gray had earlier compiled Over the Black Coffee, and this small volume does the same service for tea. Its introduction declares that tea is the drink of the world, domestically and socially, whatever statistics say about other crops.

Gray argues that no other product has been held in such high regard by writers of standing and good taste. A glance through the book, he says, shows the spirit of tea as one of peace, comfort, and refinement. Readers get a light anthology of tea praise, quotation, and lore, opened by a verse tribute from Colley Cibber.
the-moral-picture-book:
The Moral Picture Book opens with a story headed John Cooper, illustrated with scenes captioned Prayer and Affection. John Cooper, an only child living with his parents in a cottage beside a village green, owns a dog named Carlo whom he loves. His playmate Tom Jones tempts him into truancy one school day.

Tom proposes a long walk along the stream instead of lessons, hunting birds' nests in the wood. Sunshine, full leaves, butterflies, and singing birds make the outing look joyful. Only Carlo is truly happy, the narrator insists. John cannot forget he has done wrong and will grieve his kind parents, while Tom laughs loudly to smother his own bitter feelings. A mile into the wood, the boys spot a wren's nest in an old willow.
the-new-dr-price-cookbook:
The New Dr. Price Cook Book, issued for use with Dr. Price's Phosphate Baking Powder from the Price Baking Powder Factory in Chicago, is present here only in a publisher's introduction and the start of an index, so no recipes appear. The Royal Baking Powder Company held the 1921 copyright. Recipes of universal appeal, the introduction promises, were chosen to be popular in every home and useful every day of the year.

Famous recipes were made more appealing with the baking powder, the note says, while economising on eggs and other costly ingredients. New recipes were meant to suit beginners yet earn laurels for experts. The index begins with Albuminized Orange, salted almonds, Angel Cake, and apple dishes.
the-ontario-readers-fourth-book: The Ontario Readers, Fourth Book, was a school reader authorized by the Minister of Education for Ontario and entered in Canada in 1909, published by the T. Eaton Company of Toronto. The title page and the start of a contents list are present, and no lesson text follows them. The contents open with Kipling's Children's Song and Tennyson's Our Country, and list pieces by George Eliot, Shakespeare, Christina Rossetti, Stevenson, Parkman, Dickens, and the Bible.
the-ontario-readers-third-book: The Ontario Readers, Third Book, was a school reader authorized by the Minister of Education for Ontario and entered in Canada in 1909, published in Toronto by the T. Eaton Company. Only the front matter is present here, chiefly lists of thanks for permission to reprint, so the lessons themselves do not appear. The Minister thanks Kipling, Henry Newbolt, Flora Annie Steel, Charles G. D. Roberts, and Ralph Connor, among many others. A frontispiece shows the Union Jack.
the-pink-fairy-book:
The Pink Fairy Book, edited by Andrew Lang, gathers nursery tales from many parts of the world. Lang's preface observes that Japanese, Chinese, Native American, Eskimo, African, Greek, and Egyptian tellers all hand such tales to their children. The stories often resemble one another across great distances. Readers of the earlier Blue, Red, and Yellow Fairy Books will meet old friends with new faces here. They will also meet figures new to them, such as the Japanese Tanuki.

Lang names the helpers behind the volume. W. A. Craigie translated the Danish and Swedish tales. Mrs. Lang rendered the Sicilian, African, Catalan, Japanese, and old French stories through German and French versions. Alma Alleyne took the Andersen tales from the German. Mr. Ford drew the monsters, mermaids, princes, and giants. Lang closes with the fairy-tale moral that courage, youth, beauty, and kindness win in the end.
the-pirates-own-book:
Charles Ellms's The Pirates Own Book, dated 1837, offers authentic narratives of the most celebrated sea robbers. Its preface argues that few subjects stir curiosity like the desperate exploits and foul doings of pirates. Mariners, Ellms writes, hold a superstitious horror of the very name. Landsmen, meanwhile, cannot resist the tales.

The preface sketches the pirate's world in broad strokes. Crews were formed from the desperadoes of every nation. Their retreats were lonely islands or wooded shores along rivers, bays, and lagoons. The Indian Ocean, both African coasts, and the West Indies served as haunts for centuries. Captured crews and passengers were murdered, cargoes plundered, and ships destroyed so no trace remained. Between cruises, Ellms says, pirates passed their hours drinking and singing old songs among the palms of the torrid zone.
the-red-fairy-book: Andrew Lang edited a companion volume of fairy tales dedicated to Master Billy Tremayne Miles, praised as a profound student and amiable critic. Contents list twelve dancing princesses, Princess Mayblossom, Soria Moria Castle, the death of Koschei the Deathless, a master thief, an enchanted pig, Jack and the beanstalk, Rapunzel, Mother Holle, and many more. Here only the dedication and contents list are present, so the tales themselves do not appear.
the-rocket-book:
Peter Newell's picture book was copyrighted and patented in 1912 and published that October by Harper and Brothers at New York. Verse begins in a basement, where Fritz, the janitor's bad kid, finds a rocket hidden beneath a window casement, strikes a match, and lights it on the concrete.

The rocket shoots through the ceiling into the first flat, where the Steiners sit at breakfast, and smashes a catsup bottle as the family quakes. Each floor will clearly get its own disaster in rhyme. Newell's hole-through-the-book gimmick turns a firework prank into a vertical tour of an apartment house.
the-slant-book:
Peter Newell wrote and pictured The Slant Book, copyrighted by Harper and Brothers in 1910. The book itself was patented in September that year, its title page notes. A motto warns that uphill work is slow, while down the slant comes speed. The text is verse, printed to match its downhill subject.

Where Bobby lives there is a hill, the verse begins. It is so steep and high that Jack and Jill might try their famous act there. Once Bobby's go-cart broke away and kited down the hill. His careless nurse screamed in dismay, but Bobby was delighted. He clapped his hands and laughed while she pursued in hopeless consternation. An officer slid off a lid and bellowed that Bobby was scorching, the verse continues.
the-song-of-sixpence-picture-book: Walter Crane supplied the original coloured designs for this picture book, issued by John Lane in London and New York. It belongs to the series called Walter Crane's Picture Books. Here the record shows the decorated title pages and Crane's preface, dated from Kensington in September 1909. The rhymes and tales themselves lie beyond what is present.
the-spinster-book: Myrtle Reed's book of essays for unmarried women was copyrighted in 1901 and issued by G. P. Putnam's Sons of New York and London. The pages present here are front matter only. They show the 1907 Knickerbocker Press title page and a long list of reprintings between 1901 and 1907. A catalogue of Reed's other books includes Lavender and Old Lace and The Master's Violin, so the essays themselves do not appear.
the-trail-book: Mary Austin's Trail Book, published in 1918 with illustrations by Milo Winter, is dedicated to her niece Mary, in hope that the trails of her own country lead her to wonderland. This record gives the title page, dedication, and a detailed contents list. Oliver and Dorcas Jane find the trail, and then animal and Native tellers take turns: the Buffalo Chief, the Coyote, the Corn Woman, the Pelican, and an Onondaga among them. Their tellings trace mastodons, corn, salt trails, and mound-builders. Austin's stories themselves begin beyond these leaves.
the-violet-fairy-book:
Andrew Lang edits The Violet Fairy Book and insists in his preface that he did not write its stories. Ladies keep asking what else he has written besides the Fairy Books, forcing the same explanation. The tales were translated from popular traditional stories in many languages, and Lang claims them as old as anything humans invented.

His preface traces the stories from fireside tellers to civilised ancestors who believed beasts, trees, and stones could talk. Country people preserved what the rich and educated forgot, changing tales as they handed them down. Learned collectors then printed them for children. Lang dedicates the volume to Violet Myers and argues that children's tastes still match their distant ancestors, preferring fairy tales to arithmetic.
the-virginia-housewife-or-methodical-coo: Mrs. Mary Randolph's Virginia Housewife, or Methodical Cook, dated 1860, carries the motto that method is the soul of management. The material present here is a contents list, so the recipes themselves do not appear. Soups come first in long variety: asparagus, beef, gravy, veal, oyster, barley, pea, ochra, hare, catfish, and onion, plus turtle and mock turtle. A beef section follows with curing, drying, and corning directions, then beef à-la-mode, baked brisket, beef olives, stewed rump, hunter's beef, steaks, and steak pie.
the-yellow-fairy-book:
Andrew Lang edited The Yellow Fairy Book, following his Blue, Red, and Green collections. A verse dedication addresses three children by nickname. The poem teases that learning letters is hard for curly heads. Yet the alphabet, it says, guides children into Fairy Land. The path may end at the Garden of the Singing Rose. Lang's preface then addresses young readers directly.

Children, Lang expects, will forgive yet another fairy book. Adults may object to printing so many, he admits. He cares little for adult opinion if children are pleased. One gentleman critic, he notes, disapproves of the series. The tales that follow gather folklore from many lands. Lang's colour fairy books shaped childhood reading for generations.
